https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: A chilling case has emerged in South Australia, where a mother who died in a suspected murder-suicide visited a police station a day before the incident, according to South Australia Police. The bodies of 36-year-old Helena Wright and her 23-month-old daughter were found in the ocean west of Port MacDonnell on Monday (July 27, 2026).Wright, 36, visited the Mount Gambier Police Station on Sunday, July 26, where she spoke with police, authorities confirmed on Wednesday (July 29, 2026), according to The Guardian. On Wednesday, police said they had ended the official search for a missing three-month-old after “careful consideration”, saying the infant “could not have survived the period of time that has elapsed, either in the water or on land,” as quoted by The Guardian.Emergency crews were dispatched to the area on Monday after an abandoned vehicle with its engine still running was discovered at about 11.15 a.m. Wright, who was originally from Estonia, lived in Compton, a small locality outside Mount Gambier, about 26 kilometers north of Port MacDonnell.Authorities said Wright had visited a police station one day before her body was found. On the morning of the incident, at about 9.30 a.m., officers went to her home to conduct a welfare check after a concerned friend contacted police. No one was at the property when they arrived. Wright and her 23-month-old daughter were later located below the cliffs, with local fishers assisting in recovering their bodies.Investigators have spoken with Wright's husband, the father of the children, and said based on the evidence currently available, the matter is being investigated as a murder-suicide . Meanwhile, land and sea search operations were launched around Cape Northumberland near Port MacDonnell on the Limestone Coast in an effort to find the missing three-month-old infant. Comprehensive physical search efforts have focused on a sizable area of water and land, unfortunately the infant has not been found, police said on Wednesday, as quoted by The Guardian. Officers also acknowledged that hopes of finding the infant alive had faded. The reality is, after three days, the chances of finding the baby alive are zero, Supt. Trent Cox said earlier on Wednesday.Cox said rescue efforts had been complicated by extremely challenging conditions, preventing emergency vessels from entering the water for much of Tuesday and restricting search teams to the shoreline and clifftops. We've been unable to … launch water assets. We've been able to get the SES aerial drone up, he said, adding that specialists had advised against using an underwater drone because of the hazardous conditions.Police said they will continue to coordinate shoreline monitoring and inspections across the coming days . South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said the tragedy had deeply shaken the community. If it involves children, that breaks your heart, he said on Tuesday.The matter has been referred to the coroner, who will examine the cause and circumstances surrounding the deaths. Police said there is no information to suggest that any person other than the mother and her two children were involved in this heart-breaking incident .

Photograph: Alecsandra Raluca Drăgoi/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Marc Conway, a former IPP prisoner who now leads a campaign group, said Burnham’s action was ‘an essential first step’. Photograph: Alecsandra Raluca Drăgoi/The Guardian Prisons and probation Andy Burnham pledge to end indefinite prison terms ‘a step towards healing’ Campaigners welcome plan to bring IPP sentences to a close but say the move is long overdue Jamie Grierson Sun 30 Aug 2026 08.36 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Campaigners have hailed Andy Burnham’s pledge to bring an end to indefinite jail terms as “a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for”. The prime minister has said he will “end the injustice” of imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentences during this parliament, meaning people will no longer be trapped indefinitely under a sentence abolished more than a decade ago. The IPP sentence was a form of indeterminate sentence in which offenders were given a minimum jail tariff but no maximum for a range of crimes. Introduced in 2005, IPPs were designed for the indefinite detention of serious offenders who were perceived to be a risk to the public, but were used much more widely than intended and issued to offenders who committed low-level crimes. The sentence was scrapped in 2012, but its abolition was not retrospective. Those given an IPP sentence were, in addition, placed on licence indefinitely after release, and are only eligible to have their licence removed after 10 years. Statistics from the Ministry of Justice and HM Prison and Probation Service show that, as of 30 June this year, 856 people remained behind bars after being given IPP sentences. Eight out of 10 of those have been jailed for at least 10 years beyond the minimum term at which they can apply for parole. A further 1,415 IPP prisoners were recalled to custody after being released on licence, the data shows. Responding to Burnham’s announcement on Sunday, Marc Conway, a former IPP prisoner who now leads a campaign group against the sentencing regime called Ungripp, said the move was a long overdue step toward justice. Conway, who was handed an IPP sentence for armed robbery, was one of three released offenders who tackled the Fishmongers’ Hall terrorist Usman Khan in 2019 on London Bridge. He has previously spoken of his fear that tackling the terrorist may have landed him back in jail under the terms of his IPP. “This is a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for,” Conway said. “For too long, their loved ones have been trapped by a sentence that was acknowledged as flawed over a decade ago. “While we welcome this critical action by the government, we do so with heavy hearts for those who did not live to see this day, and for the families torn apart by years of endless uncertainty. Legislation alone cannot undo 20 years of damage, but it is the essential first step toward healing.” Ungripp urged the Ministry of Justice and probation services to ensure that the implementation of the decision was swift, transparent and accompanied by comprehensive community and mental health support for all those transitioning off IPP licences and out of custody. Among those to have suffered from the impact of IPP sentences was Tommy Nicol , who took his own life while serving under the now abolished regime. He was handed a minimum tariff of four years for robbery. After six years in prison, he was told he would not be eligible for another parole hearing for at least another two years. His mental health deteriorated and he died a few months after that decision. Nine months before his death, Nicol described the sentence as “psychological torture of a person who is doing 99 years” in a handwritten formal complaint. Responding to Sunday’s announcement, his sister, Donna, who has been a prominent campaigner against the IPP sentence, said: “When I heard the announcement today, my heart instantly split in two. Half of me felt a profound sense of relief for the thousands of families who have spent years living in the same horrific limbo that destroyed my family. The other half of me was crushed by the absolute, unbearable pain that this decision comes 10 years too late for my brother, Tommy. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion “While I welcome the commitment to finally bring legislation to terminate these sentences and provide an endpoint to this nightmare, my message to the government today is clear: words are not enough. Implementation must be swift, clear and compassionate. Every day this takes to enact is another day someone’s son, brother or father is driven to the brink of despair. “Nothing will ever bring Tommy back through our front door. Nothing will undo the trauma my family suffered watching him lose his life to a sentence that should never have existed. But if this announcement means that no other sister has to stand where I am standing today, then Tommy’s legacy, and the fight of every IPP family who refused to give up, will finally have achieved the justice he was denied.” How has early prison release scheme been tightened after backlash? Read more Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Burnham said he had made the “judgment” that the public would prefer offenders who have served their time being freed before those who have not, and that he had “longstanding concerns” about IPP sentences which had caused “a sense of unfairness” in some cases. He promised to apply a “commonsense” approach, and said legislation would be brought forward to end such sentences by the end of the parliament. He told BBC Breakfast: “Many of the people in this position have more than served their time. But on the scheme that I inherited, they would have remained in prison, while others who committed serious offences would have been let out early. “And we will set up a cross-party oversight group to look at how this is done, because there are still individuals who will pose a risk to communities. It does need to be done in a very careful way with regard to public safety, national security and all of those issues.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org , or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Vladimir Putin is depicted in the book as a modern-day tsar without ideology or convictions. Photograph: Alexander Nemenov/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Vladimir Putin is depicted in the book as a modern-day tsar without ideology or convictions. Photograph: Alexander Nemenov/AFP/Getty Images Vladimir Putin ‘The choice was prison or exile’: journalists who fled Russia publish grim portrait of Putin Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin, who were forced to move abroad in 2021, tell of president capable of ‘limitless cruelty’ Kim Willsher Tue 22 Sep 2026 06.58 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A t 6am on 29 June 2021, the Russian journalist Roman Badanin was woken by a knock on the door of his family’s Moscow apartment. “Come quickly, someone has scratched your car in the courtyard,” a voice shouted from outside. As he opened the door, masked men pushed their way in. Across the city, a similar raid was happening at the home of Badanin’s colleague Mikhail Rubin. The masked men were officers of the FSB , the Russian intelligence service, instruments of the “climate of fear and violence” that the journalists say Vladimir Putin has imposed on Russia in their forensically detailed biography of the Russian president. The Tsar in Person is almost 800 pages and has won the Grand Prix Strasbourg, a French literary award, whose jury said it read like a “spy novel” and praised the “courage and commitment” of the authors during decades of investigating reporting. For Badanin and Rubin, the dawn raids were a warning. As founders of the independent media project Proekt, specialising in investigative journalism, both men had been threatened, interrogated, labelled traitors and foreign agents, banned from news events and had offices searched. Other colleagues had not been so lucky: several had died suddenly or in unexplained accidents or seemingly random attacks. Rubin told the Guardian: “The first time we were threatened was in 2019 when we published an investigation into the chief of Putin’s propaganda operation. A Kremlin official warned me the consequences might be scary. Security agents visited my parents and asked them why I, their son, was selling out his country, betraying Russia.” After the FSB agents’ dawn raid, Rubin discovered his passport placed carefully on a table. “It was a message. If they’d taken it, I wouldn’t be allowed to leave the country, but they wanted me to leave so they put it where I would see it,” he said. “At the time I didn’t plan on leaving. I didn’t want to overthink the danger because I thought they were just trying to stop me working.” Less than three weeks later, the Kremlin declared Proekt an “undesirable” media outlet. “I left Moscow the next morning,” Rubin said. Badanin, who was on holiday with his family in Morocco, decided it was too dangerous for him to return. “The choice was prison or exile and I didn’t want to go to prison.” View image in fullscreen Roman Badanin (left) and Mikhail Rubin. Composite: Wikipedia and Proekt Their book, so far published only in Russian and French, charts the rise of Putin from an unremarkable clerk and undercover KGB agent at St Petersburg city hall to the Kremlin, where he has clung to power since 2000. It is not the first biography to portray the president and his circle of cronies as cruel and corrupt, but the devil is in the encyclopaedic detail. Badanin and Rubin, both former Kremlin-accredited “pool” journalists, have 40 years of investigative journalism between them and have conducted hundreds of interviews to produce a grim portrait of Putin. They depict him as a modern-day tsar, without ideology or convictions, a dictator capable of “limitless cruelty” who sees himself as above morality and laws. Rivals and opponent, or simply those who have become inconvenient, meet unexpected ends in accidents, crashes and falls, or are poisoned with toxins and radioactive particles causing agonising deaths. “These pages are the result of war and repression, of exile and the death of some of those close to us, the suffering of friends thrown in prison,” the pair write. “We hope it will contribute to destroying the circumstances that have made all this misfortune possible and defeat the person who did this with his own hands.” It is also the story of Russia from the end of the Soviet Union to today. Badanin says the book is aimed at young Russians who have no idea what their country was like before Putin took power. Unsurprisingly, it is banned by the Kremlin. Badanin told Le Monde: “We’re also targeting audiences abroad, where many myths about Putin are circulating. There’s no need to invent myths about Putin. Let the facts reveal the truth about him and his system. “The Kremlin leader has no ideology. The war in Ukraine has made this clear: this war is not an extension of his ideas, it is merely a means of staying in power.” Today, even thousands of miles from Moscow, neither journalist feels entirely safe from what they call “Putin’s death squads” dispatched to murder dissident Russians abroad to demonstrate the Kremlin’s long arms. Last year, FBI agents turned up at Badanin’s California home to warn him they had information that he was at risk of an attack “by foreign special services”. “I feel a little bit safer here than in Europe , but not completely safe,” Badanin said. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said the three waves of missiles were launched by "Russian humanitarians". This comes after US envoy Steve Witkoff called Russia's President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" following a meeting in St Petersburg on Wednesday. Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks with the US and Ukraine. The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from the scene of a destroyed retail park. More on this story.
